Metaprogram evaluation

Ally Hawkins

2025-11-25

In this notebook, we’ll generate metaprograms (MPs) for a subset samples from the SKC. This includes SCPCS000841 through SCPCS000855. Note that there were not enough cells in SCPCS000848 and SCPCS000854, so these samples are not included.

cNMF was run with k components set to 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25 and all spectra are used to generate MPs. The goal of this notebook is to identify a set of metrics that we can use to evaluate MPs.

For this particular notebook, MPs are assigned by calculating the correlation of each cNMF spectra to all other spectra and then clustering using k=12. (In the future, we could easily modify this to have a parameter for k and look across reports.)

Metaprograms should be:

  • Non-redundant
  • Composed of a mix of samples
  • Biologically interpretable

Additionally, we expect expression of these MPs to be variable within the cells of each sample, and therefore useful in identifying cell states in the original samples.

The metrics shown here will help evaluate if the identified MPs show these characteristics.

Set Up

# source in some helper functions we'll use to prep data 
# build_spectra_mtx() build_spectra_cor_df()
source("./utils/spectra-helper-functions.R")
# paths to custom geneset files we're going to use for ORA
geneset_file <- file.path("..", "genesets", "custom-gene-sets.tsv")
msigdb_geneset_file <- file.path("..", "genesets", "msigdb-gene-sets.tsv")
category_file <- file.path("..", "genesets", "gene-set-categories.tsv")
# cnmf results directory
results_dir <- fs::path("..", "ews-nf-out", "cnmf")

# directories with processed rds files and annotations output from ews-nf
data_dir <- file.path("..", "scpca-nf-out", "SCPCP000026")
annotations_dir <- file.path("..", "ews-nf-out", "annotations")

# get all the spectra files
spectra_files <- fs::dir_ls(
  path = results_dir, 
  glob = "*.gene_spectra_score.k_*.dt_*.txt", 
  recurse = TRUE
  )

# extract the unique ID for labeling
unique_ids <- stringr::str_extract(spectra_files, pattern = "SCPCL[0-9]+-SCPCS[0-9]+")
names(spectra_files) <- unique_ids
# read in and build spectra mtx
spectra_mtx <- build_spectra_mtx(spectra_files)

# get correlations
cor_mtx <- cor(spectra_mtx, method = "pearson", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

# create correlation dataframe with info about each spectra
all_cor_df <- build_spectra_cor_df(cor_mtx)

Generate metaprograms

To generate metaprograms, we’ll first cluster the spectra based on their correlation to each other. We will then get the mean weight for each gene across all spectra in the cluster, omitting NAs. The gene list will then be sorted by weight with the most important genes listed at the top of the list.

dist_mtx <- as.dist(1-cor_mtx)
tree <- hclust(dist_mtx, method = "ward.D2")
clusters <- cutree(tree, k = 12) # TODO: replace with params value
mp_cluster_list <- split(colnames(spectra_mtx), clusters)
names(mp_cluster_list) <- sprintf("MP%02d",seq(1, length(mp_cluster_list)))

# generate mps 
mp_list <- mp_cluster_list |> 
  purrr::map(\(spectra_list){
    
    mps <- rowMeans(spectra_mtx[, spectra_list, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE) |>
      sort(decreasing = TRUE)
    
  })

Redundancy of metaprograms

Here we look at the correlation of all MPs to all other MPs. Ideally, MPs are unique and non-redundant and therefore have low correlation to all other MPs.

# combine all mps into a matrix for a heatmap
# get correlation to each other
mp_mtx <- do.call(cbind, mp_list)
## Warning in cbind(...): number of rows of result is not a multiple of vector length (arg 2)
mp_cor_matrix <- cor(mp_mtx, method = "pearson", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

ComplexHeatmap::Heatmap(
  mp_cor_matrix
)

We see that generally each MP is distinct from other MPs, although there are some groups of MPs that are probably closer than others - MP9 and MP2, MP6 and MP1, and MP8, MP5 and MP4.

Next we will look at the correlation of each spectra to all other spectra within the same MP and across MPs. Ideally, the spectra within a single MP should have high correlation to each other and low correlation to spectra from other MPs.

# get a table assigning MPs to each spectra
mp_lookup <- tibble::tibble(
  spectra = names(clusters),
  metaprogram = sprintf("MP%02d",clusters)
)

# for each correlation, add in the MPs being compared and classify MP
mp_cor_df <- all_cor_df |> 
  dplyr::filter(spectra1 != spectra2) |> 
  dplyr::left_join(mp_lookup, by = c("spectra1" = "spectra")) |> 
  dplyr::rename(mp1 = metaprogram) |> 
  dplyr::left_join(mp_lookup, by = c("spectra2" = "spectra")) |> 
  dplyr::rename(mp2 = metaprogram) |>
  dplyr::mutate(within_mp = mp1 == mp2) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(MP_type = dplyr::if_else(within_mp, "Within MP", "Between MPs")) |> 
  dplyr::select(spectra1, spectra2, mp1, correlation, MP_type) |> 
  dplyr::distinct()
ggplot(mp_cor_df, aes(x = correlation, color = MP_type, fill = MP_type)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.25) +
  facet_wrap(vars(mp1), scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Within MP" = "#00274C", 
                                "Between MPs" = "#FFCB05")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Within MP" = "#00274C", 
                               "Between MPs" = "#FFCB05")) +
  xlab("Correlation") +
  ylab("Density")

Sample diversity

MPs should represent a mix of samples. This metric can be useful in filtering out any MPs that are sample-specific.

We will use Shannon’s entropy to measure the diversity of each MP where 1 indicates high diversity.

mp_df <- mp_cluster_list |> 
  purrr::imap_dfr(\(spectra_list, mp_name) {
    tibble::tibble(
      metaprogram = mp_name,
      spectra = spectra_list
    )
  }) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    sample_id = stringr::word(spectra, 1, sep = "_") |> 
      stringr::word(-1, sep = "-")
  )


mp_prop_df <- mp_df |> 
  dplyr::group_by(metaprogram, sample_id) |>
  # generate one row per mp/sample combination with the total count
  dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(), 
                   .groups = "drop_last") |> 
  # get the frequency of each sample compared to all other samples
  dplyr::mutate(p = n / sum(n),
                num_samples = dplyr::n_distinct(sample_id)
  )

sample_diversity_df <- mp_prop_df |> 
  # now the shannon index for each metaprogram 
  dplyr::summarise(
    shannon = -sum(p * log(p)), # entropy
    num_samples = unique(num_samples), # get unique value for printing
    shannon_norm = shannon / log(num_samples)
    ) |> 
  dplyr::arrange(desc(shannon_norm)) 

sample_diversity_df |> 
  DT::datatable()

The below chart shows the proportion of each spectra that corresponds to each sample.

mp_prop_df <- mp_prop_df |> 
  # ungroup before setting levels otherwise the plot doesn't work
  dplyr::ungroup() |> 
  dplyr::mutate(metaprogram = forcats::fct_reorder(metaprogram, num_samples))

ggplot(mp_prop_df, aes(x = p, y = metaprogram, fill = sample_id)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    y = "Metaprogram",
    x = "Proportion of spectra",
    fill = "Sample"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = palette.colors("alphabet", n=13))

We see the entropy values are all very close to 1 and that the MPs appear to be a good mix of samples. Some MPs are only comprised of a handful of samples, which could indicate rarer populations. The key here is that we don’t see any single-sample MPs.

Biological interpretability

Ultimately, we want to be able to easily interpret the MPs. We won’t actually annotate them here, but we will look to see how biologically distinct the MPs might be.

To do that, we’ll take the first 50 genes for all MPs and do ORA using the custom genesets we use for classifying EWS::FLI1 high and low cells and the Hallmarks collection from MSigDb.

# read in custom gene lists and EF msigdb gene sets to look at 
geneset_df <- readr::read_tsv(geneset_file)
ef_msigdb_df <- readr::read_tsv(msigdb_geneset_file)

# get the EF activated and EF repressed gene sets for classifying later
ef_category_df <- readr::read_tsv(category_file) |> 
  # custom gene sets
  dplyr::left_join(geneset_df, by = c("geneset_name" = "geneset")) |> 
  # msig genesets
  dplyr::left_join(ef_msigdb_df, by = c("geneset_name" = "name")) |> 
  # make sure we have all name info in the same column
  dplyr::mutate(geneset = dplyr::if_else(is.na(geneset), geneset_name, geneset)) |> 
  # grab the category
  dplyr::select(geneset, geneset_category) |> 
  dplyr::distinct()

ef_activated_genesets <- ef_category_df |> 
  dplyr::filter(geneset_category == "EF-activated") |> 
  dplyr::pull(geneset)

ef_repressed_genesets <- ef_category_df |> 
  dplyr::filter(geneset_category == "EF-repressed") |> 
  dplyr::pull(geneset)

# use hallmarks in addition to EF lists 
hallmarks_msigdb_df <- msigdbr::msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "H") |> 
  dplyr::select(gs_name, ensembl_gene)
# get list of categories that we need to grab from msigdb
msigdb_category_list <- ef_msigdb_df |>
  dplyr::select(category, subcategory) |>
  unique() |>
  purrr::transpose()


# list of genesets and names
geneset_list <- ef_msigdb_df$geneset |>
  purrr::set_names(ef_msigdb_df$name)

# first pull out info for each category and then pull out specific genes for geneset
ef_geneset_df <- msigdb_category_list |>
  purrr::map(\(category_list){
    # replace subcategory with default NULL
    # can't use NULL in tsv since it gets read in as a character
    if (is.na(category_list$subcategory)) {
      subcategory <- NULL
    } else {
      subcategory <- category_list$subcategory
    }
    
    msigdbr::msigdbr(
      species = "Homo sapiens",
      collection = category_list$category,
      subcollection = subcategory
    )
  }) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows() |>
  # only keep relevant gene sets
  dplyr::filter(gs_name %in% geneset_list) |> 
  dplyr::select(gs_name, ensembl_gene)

# combine into a single term2df for running GSEA and ORA
all_term_df <- geneset_df |> 
  dplyr::select(gs_name = geneset, ensembl_gene = ensembl_gene_id) |> 
  dplyr::bind_rows(ef_geneset_df) |> 
  dplyr::bind_rows(hallmarks_msigdb_df) |> 
  tidyr::drop_na()
# get the universe of HVGs across all input samples
universe <- rownames(spectra_mtx)
# run ORA using the top 200 genes
ora_results <- mp_list |> 
  purrr::map(\(scores){
    genes <- names(scores)[1:50]
    
    ora_results <- clusterProfiler::enricher(
      gene = genes,
      universe = universe,
      TERM2GENE = all_term_df
    )
  })

# combine ora results into a single dataframe
# only include genesets with pvalue < 0.05, the default by enricher 
ora_results_df <- ora_results |> 
  purrr::imap_dfr(\(result, mp_name) {
    result@result |> 
      dplyr::mutate(metaprogram = mp_name) |> 
      dplyr::filter(pvalue <= 0.05) 
  })
# print out a message about which MPs have 0 genesets 
all_mps <- names(mp_list)
missing_mps <- all_mps[!all_mps %in% unique(ora_results_df$metaprogram)] |> 
  paste0(collapse = ", ")

if(missing_mps != "") {
  glue::glue("
      <div class=\"alert alert-info\">

      No gene sets were identified as significant in the following metaprograms: 
      {missing_mps}
      </div>
    ")
  }
No gene sets were identified as significant in the following metaprograms: MP08

To evaluate if the MPs are easily interpretable, we will make a heatmap that shows the significance of each gene set across all MPs. Ideal MPs will show gene sets that are uniquely enriched in that MP instead of enriched across multiple MPs. The rows represent all significant gene sets, the columns indicate the MP, and the heatmap color indicates the -log10(pvalue) for that gene set in that MP.

Only MPs with identified gene sets will be included.

# convert ora results into a heatmap of pvalues
heatmap_mtx <- ora_results_df |> 
  dplyr::mutate(logp = -log10(p.adjust)) |> 
  dplyr::select(metaprogram, ID, logp) |> 
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = metaprogram,
    values_from = logp,
    values_fill = 0  # set missing gene sets to 0                         
  ) |> 
  tibble::column_to_rownames("ID") |> 
  as.matrix()

ComplexHeatmap::Heatmap(
  heatmap_mtx,
  name = "-log10(pvalue)",
  row_names_side = "left",
  row_dend_side = "right",
  col = circlize::colorRamp2(c(0, max(heatmap_mtx)), colors = c("white", "darkslateblue")),
  row_names_gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = 10)
) |> 
  # don't cut off super long gene set names
  ComplexHeatmap::draw(padding = unit(c(2, 6, 2, 2), "cm"))

We can also look at each of the genesets and calculate Shannon’s entropy to indicate how diverse that gene set is, e.g., how many MPs is the gene set significant in. Ideally, gene sets are unique to a MP and have values close to 0.

ora_results_df |> 
  dplyr::group_by(ID) |>
  # now the shannon index for each metaprogram 
  dplyr::summarise(
    shannon = -sum(pvalue * log(pvalue)), # entropy
    num_mps = dplyr::n_distinct(metaprogram), # get unique value for printing
    shannon_norm = shannon / log(num_mps),
    metaprograms = paste0(metaprogram, collapse = ",")
    ) |> 
  dplyr::arrange(metaprograms) |> 
  DT::datatable()

Alternatively, we can use the Jaccard similarity to index to measure how similar the list of gene sets for each MP is to all other MPs.

# helper function for getting jaccard between two vectors
calc_jaccard <- function(vec1, vec2) {
  length(intersect(vec1, vec2)) / length(union(vec1, vec2))
}


# only one list here since we will compare each MP to all other MPs
id1_list <- split(ora_results_df$ID, ora_results_df$metaprogram)
# create the grid of comparisons
cross_df <- tidyr::expand_grid(id1 = names(id1_list), id2 = names(id1_list))

# calculate a single Jaccard index for each combination using split lists & ids
jaccard_scores <- cross_df |>
  purrr::pmap_dbl(\(id1, id2){
    calc_jaccard(id1_list[[id1]], id1_list[[id2]])
  })

# add scores to the comparison grid and convert to matrix
jaccard_matrix <- cross_df |>
  dplyr::mutate(jaccard = jaccard_scores) |>
  # convert to matrix
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = "id2",
    values_from = "jaccard"
  ) |>
  tibble::column_to_rownames(var = "id1") |>
  as.matrix()

ComplexHeatmap::Heatmap(jaccard_matrix,
                        name = "Jaccard index",
                        col = circlize::colorRamp2(c(0, max(jaccard_matrix)), colors = c("white", "darkslateblue")))

Here we can see groups of MPs that have similar gene set lists, such as MP11 and MP12 or MP4 and MP9.

We know that these tumor cells should show have a group of cells with a EWS::FLI1 repressed cell signature, or “low”, as we have been calling them. To see if any of these MPs show that signature, we’ll get a score for whether or not that MP shows a high or low signature. This is calculated by getting the sum of all significant gene sets in either the EF-activated or EF-repressed gene sets and then dividing by the total number of gene sets in that group.

ora_results_df |> 
  dplyr::mutate(ef_high = ID %in% ef_activated_genesets,
                ef_low = ID %in% ef_repressed_genesets) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    ef_high_score = round(sum(ef_high)/length(ef_activated_genesets), 2),
    ef_low_score = round(sum(ef_low)/length(ef_repressed_genesets),2),
    .by = "metaprogram"
  )
##    metaprogram ef_high_score ef_low_score
## 1         MP01             0          0.0
## 2         MP02             0          0.0
## 3         MP03             0          0.0
## 4         MP04             0          0.0
## 5         MP05             0          0.0
## 6         MP06             0          0.5
## 7         MP07             0          0.0
## 8         MP09             0          0.0
## 9         MP10             0          0.0
## 10        MP11             0          0.0
## 11        MP12             0          0.0

It looks like MP6 shows some enrichment of EF-low targets and MP1 has some high targets.

Using metaprograms to identify cell states

Ultimately we want to be able to use these MPs to identify cell states in our original data. In order to do that, we need to assign a score to each cell for each MP and then use that to pull out cells with high scores for that MP. Good MPs should show variation in scores across samples.

For right now, we’ll assign a score for each cell by getting the dot product between the weights for the top 50 genes in the MP and the normalized gene expression values.

# first we need to grab the sce files
# get the unique ids for only those that are present in the cNMF spectra
# this makes sure we don't try to read in any empty processed files for samples with too few cells
unique_ids <- all_cor_df |> 
  dplyr::pull(sample1) |> 
  unique()

sample_ids <- stringr::word(unique_ids, 2, sep = "-")
sce_files <- file.path(
  data_dir, 
  sample_ids,
  glue::glue("{unique_ids}_processed.rds"))

sce_list <- sce_files |> 
  purrr::map(readr::read_rds) |> 
  purrr::set_names(sample_ids)
# don't forget that we only want to look at tumor cells so we need the annotations
annotation_files <- file.path(
  annotations_dir,
  sample_ids,
  glue::glue("{unique_ids}_annotations.tsv")
) |> 
  purrr::set_names(sample_ids)

annotations_df <- annotation_files |> 
  purrr::map(readr::read_tsv) |> 
  dplyr::bind_rows(.id = "sample_id") |> 
  dplyr::select(barcodes, sample_id, annotation_tier0) |> 
  dplyr::filter(stringr::str_detect(annotation_tier0, "tumor"))
## Warning: One or more parsing issues, call `problems()` on your data frame for details, e.g.:
##   dat <- vroom(...)
##   problems(dat)
# get a dataframe with scores for each cell for each MP
score_df <- sce_list |> 
  purrr::imap_dfr(\(sce, id) {
    
    # we only care about tumor cells here
    tumor_cells <- annotations_df |> 
      dplyr::filter(sample_id == id) |> 
      dplyr::pull(barcodes)
    
    # get the genes that are detected and part of spectra
    detected_genes <- rownames(sce)[rowData(sce)$detected > 0]
    shared_genes <- intersect(detected_genes, universe)
    
    # extract counts for genes and cells of interest
    expr <- logcounts(sce)[shared_genes,tumor_cells] 
    
    # get a score for each MP 
    purrr::imap_dfr(
      mp_list,
      \(mp_vec, mp_name) {
        
        # mp specific genes 
        mp_genes <- intersect(names(mp_vec), detected_genes)
        
        # pull weights in correct cell order
        w <- mp_vec[mp_genes]
        
        # expression subset: genes × cells
        sub_expr <- expr[mp_genes, , drop = FALSE]
        
        # compute dot product for each cell (matrix multiply)
        scores <- as.numeric(w %*% sub_expr)
        
        tibble::tibble(
          sample_id = id,
          barcodes = colnames(expr),
          metaprogram = mp_name,
          dot_score = scores
        )
      }
    )
  })

First we look at the score distribution for all samples for each metaprogram. Good MPs will show variability within the dataset, in particular we are looking for a bimodal distribution.

ggplot(score_df, 
       aes(x = dot_score, y = metaprogram)) +
  ggridges::geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.8, color = "white") +
  #facet_wrap(vars(sample_id), scales = "free_x", ncol = 4) +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey90"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.position = "none"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Score across all samples",
    y = "Sample"
  )
## Picking joint bandwidth of 0.00878

Now, look at the distribution of each sample individually. Good MPs should show variability in multiple samples.

ggplot(score_df, 
       aes(x = dot_score, y = sample_id, fill = sample_id)) +
  ggridges::geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.8, color = "white", bw = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(vars(metaprogram), scales = "free_x", ncol = 4) +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey90"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.position = "none"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = palette.colors("alphabet", n=13)) +
  labs(
    x = "Score",
    y = "Sample",
    title = "MP scores by sample"
  )

It looks like we do see some good MPs with a lot of variability across a large number of samples (MP1), some programs that are heterogenous across samples like MP8 and MP6, and programs that don’t have a lot of variation, MP12. It’s likely that MP12 is not super informative here.

Finally, we’ll measure the variance of each MP in each sample and plot that in a sina plot. Good MPs will have high variance.

# calculate the variance for each MP in each sample
mp_var_df <- score_df |>
  dplyr::group_by(sample_id, metaprogram) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    variance = stats::var(dot_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(
  mp_var_df,
  aes(
    x = metaprogram,
    y = variance
  )
) +
  ggforce::geom_sina(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(
    x = "Metaprogram",
    y = "Variance of MP across all cells in a sample"
  )
